o: Explain the core ideas of programming: files, sql and strings using accurate OCR terminology.
Apply a clear method to the worked and guided questions.
Use Code First and unseen exam practice to demonstrate independent understanding.
c: The same three pupils can appear as CSV text lines, a 2D table and a typed SQL database. The representation changes, not the facts.
A 2D array uses indexes for cell access; a loop and IF are needed to select every row satisfying a condition.
SELECT chooses displayed fields, FROM names the table and WHERE selects matching records.
Loading CSV rows into an array and converting string marks into numbers is an ambitious extension; start with a supplied array for core work.

m.title: Programming: Files, SQL and Strings
m.q: Compare SQL and code for the shared Pupils table. Show why 'SELECT Name FROM Pupils WHERE Mark >= 50' returns Ada and Mia.
st: Read marks 72, 43 and 81 from the Pupils table; identify that 50 is the minimum included mark.
SQL SELECT Name requests only the Name field; WHERE Mark >= 50 keeps Ada and Mia.
In code, loop through aligned names=['Ada','Ben','Mia'] and numeric marks=[72,43,81]; test each mark>=50.
Print names[0] and names[2]. The code and SQL give the same set of names, although ordering is not guaranteed by SQL without ORDER BY.

wSteps: Check 72, 43 and 81 against the new limit of 60.
The only matching row is Ben with mark 43.
SQL: SELECT Name FROM Pupils WHERE Mark < 60;.
Equivalent code loops through indexes 0–2 and prints the name only when marks[i] < 60; output Ben.

k.q: Predict the two names printed, in code execution order.
k.code:
array names = ["Ada", "Ben", "Mia"]
array marks = [72, 43, 81]
for i = 0 to 2
    if marks[i] >= 50 then
        print(names[i])
    endif
next i

e: Write SQL to display Name from Pupils for pupils whose Mark >= 70. [3 marks]
SELECT Name [1] FROM Pupils [1] WHERE Mark >= 70 [1]; Ada and Mia match.
Complete a code condition so that names[i] is printed only when marks[i] < 50. State the result using the shared data. [3 marks]
IF marks[i] < 50 THEN [2 for correct condition/control] print(names[i]) [1]; prints Ben.
Explain why comparing '72' directly with numeric 50 can be problematic when reading marks from a CSV text file. [3 marks]
readLine() supplies text [1]; '72' is a string, while 50 is numeric [1]; the field must be converted/validated before a numerical comparison [1].

Open, read/write and close files in the appropriate mode.
SELECT selects fields, FROM selects table and WHERE filters rows.

x: SQL SELECT identifies the table to search.
r: Explain one difference between a function and a procedure.
A function returns a value; a procedure performs statements without necessarily returning a value.
Identify the fault in if age >= 13 OR age <= 18 for acceptance age 13–18.
Use AND, not OR; OR incorrectly accepts values outside the range.
Write SQL to display Name from Students where Year=10.
SELECT Name FROM Students WHERE Year = 10;
Explain how to count even values in an array.
Iterate each element; if value MOD 2 = 0 then increment counter; output counter.

stretch.task: Change the program and the SQL query to return names where Mark < 60. Write down both results and check that they match.

stretch.answer: Code prints Ben; SQL SELECT Name FROM Pupils WHERE Mark < 60; also returns Ben.

mastery.task: Optional integration: read pupils.csv, skip the header, split each line, validate/cast Mark, build a table-like structure and return pupils with numeric Mark >= 50. Compare the result with SQL, and explain how erroneous data should be handled.
mastery.hint: Use file open/read/close, split on comma in the chosen high-level language, convert numeric fields safely, then loop/filter. Only attempt after the core loop is secure.
mastery.answer: Expected names Ada and Mia. Ben 43 is excluded. A correct outline opens file; discards ID,Name,Mark header; reads/splits each row; checks number fields; converts mark to integer; tests >=50; prints corresponding names; closes file; rejects or reports malformed/non-numeric data. The SQL result contains the same names, with no guaranteed order.
